meta.notes: Reddit (r/mindbody, r/pilates, r/gymowner) blocks Preuve's fetcher, so owner voices come secondhand from a competitor's (Vibefam) roundup that quotes threads verbatim; treat those as vendor-curated. Capterra/G2, Glofox, Gleantap, Zen Planner and gymdesk pages were blocked or rate-limited, so Glofox, Zen Planner and Gleantap have no first-hand evidence here. Much of the evidence on both sides is vendor marketing (competitors selling switches; Mindbody defending). No first-hand data on how often owners review attendance or on manager budget authority. 20 prospects (all US, primary ICP); sizes only where the studio states staff/teacher counts (4); contacts only where name+title appear on the studio's own page (11 people at 10 studios); one printed email (Marz Aerial). Several studios use Squarespace subdomains because that is the fetchable canonical URL. Full Circle Yoga is likely below the 50-member floor and Yoga Sanctuary is a nonprofit. No ICP id was returned by context, so icp_id is null.

summary.statement: The main platforms already ship automated lapse detection or win-back: Mindbody's '45 Day reengagement' automation and churn-prediction models, PushPress's daily at-risk workflow, and WellnessLiving's win-back automations (launched April 2026).
Operators say personalized outreach is their top retention approach (56% in Mindbody's 2025 survey), and vendor guidance still describes hand-written check-in emails and tagging lapsed members.
Retention is part of front-desk duties in at least one Pilates job posting, done with the owner-operator through a CRM.
Add-on vendors give anecdotes of studios whose lapsed members got no follow-up, but these come from the vendors themselves.
No source says what share of small studios actually turn on the built-in automations or keep them up to date.

Leaving Mindbody involves a formal card-data (PAN) release that takes 3-4 weeks, paid export services for fuller data (a $499 fee is quoted secondhand), exporters that can time out, and reports missing on basic plans.
Card migration can fail, and some migration paths have the studio collect members' cards again by hand.
Contracts of 12/24/36 months auto-renew without notice, though month-to-month plans with a 90-day minimum also exist.

Arketa, Walla, bsport and Mindbody itself all advertise migration (including cards, in Walla's case) as free or included, and a small studio reports a full Mindbody-to-Momence transfer. A paid migration service would be competing against free.
The card problem is mostly specific to Mindbody: Stripe-based platforms such as Glofox may need no card transfer.
Secondhand and vendor sources describe weekly pulls of Mindbody data into Google Sheets and several hours a week spent exporting data for campaigns.
46% of US studio owners in a Hapana survey use their CRM for customer reports and analytics.
No first-hand count of how often owners review attendance specifically to find lapsed members was found.

Reported switching triggers include price rises (some unannounced), paid add-ons, and ownership changes: private-equity owners in general, Momence's 2025 acquisition, and the 2026 Playlist-EGYM merger.
Auto-renewing fixed terms make the contract end date a predictable decision point.
Mindbody now advertises a $79/month US entry price, and 57% of owners say new technology creates operational challenges. Both work against urgency to switch or add tools.
Member affordability pressure (61% of owners) makes churn a live concern.
The studio owner is the gate for any Mindbody integration: activating an add-on needs an action only the owner can take.
In small studios the owner often also runs the front desk or office (an 'Owner Operator + Office Manager').
No evidence was found on how much software spending studio managers can approve on their own.
Retention add-ons that sit on top of the platform already exist: DailyStory, FitGrid win-backs, APIANT's Mindbody-to-Keap sync, and Carly (waitlist fill, first-visit and lapse follow-up).
Mindbody's own cost model puts separate email/SMS tools at $75-$250/month, and its automated campaigns sit in the top Ultimate tier.
86% of US studio owners use a CRM and 37% of operators send SMS at least monthly.

hypothesis_update.problem: Independent studios still lose members who quietly lapse, but their main platforms (Mindbody, PushPress, WellnessLiving) now ship lapse detection and win-back automations, often gated to higher tiers. Migration off Mindbody is slow mainly because of card-data release, but destination vendors already do migration for free.
hypothesis_update.users: Studio owners, studio managers, and desk staff handling member outreach.
hypothesis_update.economic_value: Recovering a few lapsed members a month (illustratively $200-$400/month for a ~300-member studio); migration savings are captured by free vendor onboarding.

rationale.statement: Native retention automations exist at Mindbody, PushPress and WellnessLiving, with Mindbody's full campaigns in its Ultimate tier.
Arketa, Walla, bsport and Mindbody advertise free migration, so a paid migration service competes with free.
An illustrative vendor model puts recovered revenue at $200-$400/month for a 320-member studio.

new_unknowns.question: What share of independent studios on Mindbody Starter/Accelerate (without Ultimate automations) would pay $49-$99/month for win-back on top, given the illustrative recovered revenue of a few hundred dollars a month?
Do studios on Mindbody, PushPress or WellnessLiving actually turn on and maintain the native win-back automations, and if not, why?

current_solutions.statement: Most studios rely on their core platform. Mindbody, PushPress and WellnessLiving each already include lapse detection or win-back automations, at least on some tiers.
Personalized outreach by the owner or desk staff is the most-cited retention approach, sometimes supported by spreadsheets.
Add-on vendors (DailyStory, FitGrid, Carly, APIANT/Keap) already sell retention automation on Mindbody data.
Platform migration is usually done for free by the destination vendor's onboarding team, with Mindbody card release as the slowest step.
